relearning.title: Read: atoms, molecules and bonds
relearning.description: A short reading with the LEGO analogy, worked examples and quick checks.

body.text:
**I can describe atoms, elements, molecules, compounds, and types of chemical bonds.**

**Think of LEGO bricks.** One brick is an **atom**, the smallest unit. A bag of only red bricks is like an **element**: only one kind of atom. Snap two or more bricks together and you have a **molecule**. If the bricks you snapped together are different colors, it is a **compound**.

**Inside an atom.** The **nucleus** in the center holds **protons** (positive charge) and **neutrons** (no charge). **Electrons** (negative charge) move in the space around the nucleus. The **atomic number** is the number of protons, and it decides which element the atom is. A neutral atom has the same number of electrons as protons.

**Element:** a pure substance made of only one kind of atom, like carbon (C) or oxygen (O).
**Molecule:** two or more atoms bonded together, like O₂ or H₂O.
**Compound:** two or more **different** elements bonded together, like H₂O or CO₂.

Every compound is made of different elements, but not every molecule is a compound. O₂ is a molecule (two atoms bonded) but not a compound (only one element).

**Worked example:** CO₂ has 1 carbon atom and 2 oxygen atoms bonded together, so it is a **molecule**. It has two different elements, so it is also a **compound**. Helium (He) is a single atom of one element, so it is an **element** only.

checks.prompt: Which one is a molecule but NOT a compound?
checks.explanation: Cl₂ is two chlorine atoms bonded together, so it is a molecule, but it has only one element, so it is not a compound. CH₄ and C₆H₁₂O₆ have different elements, so they are both. Thinking every molecule is a compound is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: A neutral atom has 8 protons. How many electrons does it have? Type a number.
checks.explanation: In a neutral atom the positive protons and negative electrons balance, so 8 protons means 8 electrons. Counting neutrons is the common mistake: they have no charge.

sections.title: Ions and the two kinds of bonds

body.text:
**Ions.** An atom that gains or loses electrons is no longer balanced, so it has a charge. It is now an **ion**. Lose electrons and it becomes **positive** (more protons than electrons). Gain electrons and it becomes **negative**. Its protons don't change, so it is still the same element.

**Covalent bonds: sharing.** Think of two friends both holding the same rope. In a covalent bond, two atoms **share** electrons. Water, glucose and most molecules in living things are held together by covalent bonds.

**Ionic bonds: giving.** Think of magnets. In an ionic bond, one atom **gives** electrons to another. That makes one positive ion and one negative ion, and opposite charges attract. Table salt forms this way: sodium gives 1 electron to chlorine, making Na⁺ and Cl⁻.

**Worked example 2:** An atom has 12 protons, 12 neutrons and 10 electrons. Charge = protons − electrons = 12 − 10 = **+2**. It is a positive ion (Mg²⁺). The neutrons don't count, because they have no charge.

**Worked example 3:** In O₂, two oxygen atoms share electrons. Neither one gives electrons away, so the bond is **covalent**.

**CHNOPS.** The six most common elements in living things are carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, phosphorus and sulfur.

**Watch out for:** putting electrons in the nucleus, thinking every molecule is a compound, counting neutrons when finding the charge, mixing up sharing (covalent) and giving (ionic), and thinking that gaining or losing electrons changes the element.

checks.prompt: An atom has 17 protons, 18 neutrons and 18 electrons. What is its charge?
checks.explanation: Charge = protons − electrons = 17 − 18 = −1. It has one extra electron, so it is a negative ion (Cl⁻). Counting the 18 neutrons is the common mistake: neutrons have no charge.

checks.prompt: In a molecule of ammonia (NH₃), the nitrogen atom and the hydrogen atoms share electrons. What kind of bond is this?
checks.explanation: Sharing electrons is a covalent bond. An ionic bond gives electrons away. A hydrogen bond is a weak attraction between different molecules, not a bond inside one. Picking hydrogen bond because the atoms are hydrogen is the common mistake.

sections.shortAnswer: Explain the difference between a covalent bond and an ionic bond, and give one example of each.

relearning.description: Flashcards with a 3-question self-quiz, then a worked problem one step at a time.

cards.back: The smallest unit of matter that still has the properties of an element.
Proton: positive, in the nucleus. Neutron: no charge, in the nucleus. Electron: negative, moving around the nucleus.
A pure substance made of only one kind of atom, like carbon or oxygen. The number of protons decides which element it is.
Two or more atoms bonded together, like O₂ or H₂O.
Two or more different elements bonded together, like H₂O or CO₂. O₂ is not a compound.
An atom that gained or lost electrons, so it has a charge. Lose electrons: positive. Gain electrons: negative.
Covalent: atoms share electrons. Ionic: one atom gives electrons to another, and the opposite charges attract.

checks.explanation: Iron is made of only one kind of atom, so it is an element. Water and table salt each have two different elements bonded together, so they are compounds.

checks.prompt: Which one is BOTH a molecule and a compound?
checks.explanation: CO₂ has atoms bonded together (a molecule) from two different elements (a compound). O₂ has only one element, and Ne is a single atom. Calling O₂ a compound is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: A magnesium atom gives two electrons to an oxygen atom. What kind of bond forms?
checks.explanation: Giving electrons makes a positive ion and a negative ion that attract: an ionic bond. A covalent bond shares electrons instead. Mixing up giving and sharing is the common mistake.

sections.title: Worked problem: from atom to ion

body.problem: A sodium atom has 11 protons, 12 neutrons and 11 electrons. To make table salt, it gives 1 electron to a chlorine atom, which has 17 protons and 17 electrons. Describe both atoms before and after, and name the bond.

steps.text: Find the element. 11 protons means atomic number 11, which is sodium (Na). The number of protons decides the element.
Find the charge before. 11 protons (+) and 11 electrons (−) balance, so the charge is 0. It is a neutral atom. Neutrons have no charge, so they don't count.
After giving away 1 electron, sodium has 11 protons and 10 electrons. Charge = 11 − 10 = +1. It is now a positive ion, Na⁺. It is still sodium, because its protons did not change.
Chlorine gained that electron: 17 protons and 18 electrons. Charge = 17 − 18 = −1. It is now a negative ion, Cl⁻.
Name the bond. An electron was given away, and the opposite charges attract, so this is an ionic bond. Together they make NaCl.

checks.prompt: Your turn: a calcium atom has 20 protons and 20 electrons. It loses 2 electrons. What is its charge? Type it like +1 or −1.
checks.explanation: After losing 2 electrons it has 20 protons and 18 electrons. Charge = 20 − 18 = +2. Losing negative electrons makes the charge positive, not negative, which is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: In which case do the atoms share electrons instead of giving them away?
checks.explanation: Two atoms of the same element can't pull an electron away from each other, so they share: a covalent bond. In KCl and NaF, the metal gives an electron to the nonmetal, making an ionic bond.
